title: FAR U5·W4 — Consolidated Financial Statements: Eliminations & Noncontrolling Interest
lessonHtml:
Cold open — one economic entity

When a parent controls a subsidiary, GAAP requires consolidated financial statements that present the two as a single economic entity. BAR Unit 1 covered the acquisition-date accounting (ASC 805 — fair values, goodwill, measuring noncontrolling interest); this week covers the ongoing consolidation procedures — combining the books, eliminating intercompany transactions, and reporting the noncontrolling interest. For a multi-entity group like MBG and its affiliates, this is how the separate ledgers become one set of statements.

When to consolidate

Consolidation is required when one entity has a controlling financial interest in another — generally more than 50% of the voting interest, or being the primary beneficiary of a variable interest entity (VIE) (the party with power over the activities that most affect performance and exposure to its losses/returns). Control, not mere ownership percentage, is the trigger. Below control, the investment is reported under the equity method (significant influence) or as a financial asset, as covered in FAR Unit 2 — consolidation applies only when control exists.

The consolidation process

Consolidation combines 100% of the subsidiary's assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses with the parent's — even when the parent owns less than 100% — and then removes the double-counting through elimination entries made only on the consolidation worksheet (never on the separate books). The first elimination removes the parent's investment account against the subsidiary's equity at acquisition, establishing any goodwill and the noncontrolling interest. The remaining eliminations remove the effects of transactions between the affiliated companies, because a single economic entity cannot transact with itself.

Noncontrolling interest

The noncontrolling interest (NCI) is the portion of a subsidiary's equity not owned by the parent. Under current GAAP it is reported within consolidated equity — separately from the parent's equity — not as a liability or mezzanine item. Each period, consolidated net income is split between the amount attributable to the parent and the amount attributable to the NCI (the NCI's ownership percentage of the subsidiary's net income, adjusted for any fair-value depreciation and downstream/upstream profit). Total consolidated net income includes both shares; only the parent's portion flows to the parent's retained earnings.

Eliminating intercompany balances

The simplest eliminations remove intercompany balances and transactions that net to zero for the combined entity. Intercompany receivables and payables (a loan between parent and subsidiary) are eliminated against each other. Intercompany sales and the related cost of goods sold are eliminated so consolidated revenue reflects only sales to outside parties. Intercompany dividends paid by the subsidiary to the parent are eliminated. None of these affect consolidated net income on their own — they simply prevent inflating both sides of the statements with internal activity.

Unrealized intercompany inventory profit

The harder eliminations involve unrealized profit still inside the group. When one affiliate sells inventory to another at a markup and the buyer has not yet resold it to an outside party, the profit is unrealized and must be deferred — eliminated from consolidated income and from ending inventory. Worked example: the parent sells inventory costing $60,000 to the subsidiary for $100,000; if the subsidiary still holds it at year-end, the $40,000 intercompany profit is eliminated, reducing consolidated inventory to its original $60,000 cost. The profit is recognized only when the goods are sold outside the group.

Intercompany fixed assets and bonds

Two other unrealized items recur. On an intercompany sale of a depreciable fixed asset, the gain is eliminated at the date of sale and then realized gradually as the buyer depreciates the asset (an adjustment each year over its remaining life). On intercompany bonds — when one affiliate buys the other's debt from the market — the bonds are treated as retired in the consolidated statements, and any difference between the purchase price and carrying amount is a gain or loss on constructive retirement. Both ensure the consolidated entity reports only transactions with the outside world.

Upstream versus downstream

The direction of an intercompany sale matters for the NCI. A downstream sale (parent to subsidiary) generates profit on the parent's books, so deferred profit reduces only the parent's share of income. An upstream sale (subsidiary to parent) generates profit on the subsidiary's books, so the deferred unrealized profit is allocated between the parent and the NCI in proportion to ownership. Getting the direction right is what makes the split of consolidated net income between parent and NCI correct — a frequently tested nuance.

The consolidation worksheet

In practice, consolidation is performed on a worksheet that lists the parent and subsidiary trial balances in adjacent columns, adds elimination columns (debits and credits), and extends to a consolidated column. The eliminations are not posted to either company's books — they exist only on the worksheet and are re-created each period because the separate ledgers still contain the intercompany amounts. A common beginning-of-year elimination reverses the prior period's deferred profit so it is realized in the year the inventory is finally sold outside, keeping the cumulative consolidated income correct across periods.

Combined statements and push-down accounting

Two related presentations round out consolidation. Combined financial statements present entities under common control (e.g., affiliated companies owned by the same individual) without a parent-subsidiary relationship — using the same intercompany eliminations but no investment-elimination entry. Push-down accounting lets an acquired subsidiary restate its own books to the acquisition-date fair values, so its separate statements already reflect the new basis. Both are tools for presenting related entities faithfully, and both rest on the same elimination discipline that prevents a group from counting internal activity as real results.

Mid-year acquisitions and preacquisition earnings

When a subsidiary is acquired during the year, the consolidated income statement includes the subsidiary's revenues and expenses only from the acquisition date forward — the subsidiary's preacquisition earnings are excluded from consolidated net income. The balance sheet, however, consolidates the subsidiary in full at year-end, and the noncontrolling interest's share of income is likewise measured only on post-acquisition results. This timing convention ensures the group reports only the results it actually controlled, and it is a common exam wrinkle layered on top of the elimination mechanics.

CMA bridge

MBG's intercompany loans, equipment transfers, and material sales among affiliated entities are exactly the transactions these eliminations remove. The CMA program tracks the separate-entity results; FAR consolidation shows the group's true position to outside lenders by stripping out everything the affiliates did with each other — the same reciprocal-account discipline used in intercompany reconciliations.

Practice and recap

  1. Consolidate when control exists (>50% voting or VIE primary beneficiary); combine 100% of the subsidiary even if less than wholly owned.
  2. Eliminate the investment against subsidiary equity (establishing goodwill and NCI); report NCI within consolidated equity and split net income between parent and NCI.
  3. Eliminate intercompany receivables/payables, sales/COGS, and dividends; defer unrealized intercompany inventory profit until resold outside.
  4. Eliminate intercompany fixed-asset gains (realize over depreciation) and treat intercompany bonds as constructively retired; allocate upstream (not downstream) deferred profit between parent and NCI.

Recap: consolidation applies when a parent controls a subsidiary (>50% voting or VIE primary beneficiary), combining 100% of the subsidiary while eliminating the investment against its equity to establish goodwill and the noncontrolling interest, which sits within consolidated equity; intercompany receivables/payables, sales/COGS, and dividends are eliminated, and unrealized intercompany profit in inventory (a $40,000 markup still on hand) and fixed-asset gains are deferred until realized outside the group, with upstream deferrals — unlike downstream — shared between the parent and the NCI.

flashcards.back: A controlling financial interest: >50% of voting interest, OR being the primary beneficiary of a VIE (power + exposure to losses/returns). Control, not just ownership %, is the trigger.

flashcards.front: Consolidation combines how much of the sub?
flashcards.back: 100% of the subsidiary's assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses — even if the parent owns less than 100% — then eliminate intercompany items on the worksheet only.
The portion of the subsidiary's equity not owned by the parent; reported WITHIN consolidated equity (not a liability). Consolidated net income is split between parent and NCI.
Intercompany receivables/payables, intercompany sales/COGS, and intercompany dividends — so consolidated statements show only transactions with outside parties.
Defer profit on intercompany inventory still held at year-end. Parent sells $60k-cost goods for $100k; sub still holds → eliminate $40k profit, restate inventory to $60k. Recognize when sold outside.
Eliminate the gain at the sale date; realize it gradually as the buyer depreciates the asset over its remaining life.
When one affiliate buys the other's bonds, treat them as constructively retired; difference between price and carrying value = gain/loss on constructive retirement.
Downstream (parent→sub): deferred profit reduces only the parent's income. Upstream (sub→parent): deferred profit is shared between parent and NCI by ownership %.

questions.q: Consolidated financial statements are required when the parent has:
choices: A controlling financial interest (>50% voting or VIE primary beneficiary)
questions.explain: Control — generally >50% of voting interest or being a VIE's primary beneficiary — triggers consolidation.

questions.q: When a parent owns 80% of a subsidiary, consolidation combines:
choices: 100% of the subsidiary, with a 20% noncontrolling interest
questions.explain: Consolidation combines 100% of the subsidiary; the 20% not owned is the noncontrolling interest.

choices: Within consolidated equity, separate from the parent's equity
questions.explain: Under current GAAP, NCI is a component of consolidated equity, shown separately from the parent's equity.

questions.q: Parent sells inventory costing $60,000 to its subsidiary for $100,000; the subsidiary still holds it at year-end. The consolidation entry:
choices: Eliminates the $40,000 unrealized profit and restates inventory to $60,000
questions.explain: Unrealized intercompany profit ($40,000) is deferred until the goods are sold outside the group; inventory is restated to original cost.

questions.q: An intercompany gain on the sale of a depreciable fixed asset is:
choices: Eliminated at sale and realized over the asset's remaining depreciation
questions.explain: The gain is eliminated at the date of sale and realized gradually as the buyer depreciates the asset.

questions.q: Deferred unrealized profit on an UPSTREAM sale (subsidiary to parent) is:
choices: Allocated between the parent and the NCI by ownership
questions.explain: Upstream profit arises on the subsidiary's books, so the deferral is shared between parent and NCI; downstream affects only the parent.

questions.q: Intercompany receivables and payables between a parent and subsidiary are:
questions.explain: Intercompany balances are eliminated so the consolidated entity does not report amounts owed to itself.
